text: He pushed for more police, leaned on landlords, enforced building codes building by building, and started assembling the legal machinery to clear and rebuild large pieces of Hyde Park and Kenwood.
He said the very life of the university was at stake.
And Levi understood something most reformers didn't.
The fastest way to change a place was to change the law underneath it.
So he went further than rhetoric.
He helped write the laws he needed.
In 1953 Illinois passed an Urban Community Conservation Act that let a neighborhood be designated for conservation and replanning, and Levi was deeply involved in shaping it.

A few years later he worked with the presidents of Harvard, Yale, Penn, and MIT to get Section 112 added to the federal Housing Act of 1959, a provision that let a university's own spending near its campus count toward the local share of a federal renewal grant.
The university wasn't just participating in urban renewal.
It was building the tools the whole country would use.
Hyde Park became one of the first large urban communities in the country to undergo this kind of planned clearance at its own request, and that was Levi's design.
